drapeaux.note: French terms “négociants-fabricants”, “chefs d'atelier”, “compagnons”, “maîtres-gardes” are glossed in English at first occurrence; “prud'hommes” kept as the established term.
The repère summarizes the 1806 law as presented by the French Ministry of Justice page; the law's own wording was not retrieved in English (no official English translation found).

titre: Lyon, 1806: The First Conseil de Prud'hommes, Five Votes to Four
accroche: The law of March 18, 1806 creates a silk-industry court in Lyon. Nine elected judges, five of them manufacturers: long before parity, labor justice already tilts.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1805, Napoleon passes through Lyon, where the silk industry is drained after the upheavals of the Revolution. He promises swift measures. The *négociants-fabricants* (merchant-manufacturers), the merchants who order silk and sell it, have been demanding for years that some regulation of the trade be restored. A project for a jury with powers judged excessive had already been set aside in 1801 by the minister Chaptal. A council of a new kind is finally accepted: the law of March 18, 1806 establishes in Lyon a *conseil de prud'hommes* (a trade tribunal of peers), the first of its kind in France.

The council has nine members. Five are merchant-manufacturers. Four are *chefs d'atelier* (master weavers), the masters who own their looms, work to order, and employ journeymen. The members are elected. One must be at least thirty, have six years' practice of the trade, and be able to read and write; to vote, being twenty-five is enough.

The council conciliates, then judges disputes between manufacturers and master weavers. Before it, these disputes fell to the justice of the peace or to the police authorities, who were criticized for lacking professional competence. The council is meant to replace the old body of the *maîtres-gardes* (guild wardens), in a new form: in 1801, Chaptal had denounced in the planned jury the power to impose arbitrary fines and to conduct searches. A supplementary decree of July 3, 1806 specifies how it works.

## A labor court, but not a workers' court

The word “prud'hommes” today evokes employees and employers on an equal footing. That is not the foundation of 1806. Journeymen, the workers without a workshop of their own, have no seat there as such. Manufacturers have one more judge than master weavers: five to four. Parity arrives only with the law of May 27, 1848, under the Second Republic.

The model, for its part, spreads quickly. Under the First Empire, the institution takes root in some thirty cities, including Rouen (as early as 1807), Saint-Étienne, Nîmes, and Lille; as early as 1808, councils are also created in a dozen European cities, from Aachen to Rome. Around 1847, there are about seventy-five of them.

What the law of 1806 invents is a court whose judges come from the trade they judge. The question it leaves open is which trades sit there, and with how many votes.

repere.texte: The law of March 18, 1806 creates in Lyon a conseil de prud'hommes of nine members: five merchant-manufacturers and four master weavers, each having to show six years' practice of his trade.
repere.source: French Ministry of Justice, “Bicentenary of the Lyon Conseil des prud'hommes” (archives)

carte.punch: The first conseil de prud'hommes (1806) had five employers to four master weavers.
carte.idee: The law of March 18, 1806 creates in Lyon a silk-industry court of nine elected judges: five manufacturers and four master weavers. Parity between employers and employees arrives only with the law of May 27, 1848.
carte.source_courte: Law of March 18, 1806 · Ministry of Justice

quiz.question: Why was the 1806 Lyon conseil de prud'hommes not a parity court?
choix: Manufacturers held five of the nine seats, against four for master weavers
Only career magistrates sat on it, alongside a single manufacturer
Journeymen held the majority, but the prefect could overturn their decisions
The council only judged disputes between manufacturers, with no master weaver present
quiz.explication: The council had five manufacturers and four master weavers, all elected and drawn from the trade; parity dates from the law of 1848. Career magistrates did not sit on it, and the disputes pitted manufacturers against master weavers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How old must one be to vote in the Lyon council elections in 1806?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that to vote, being twenty-five is enough. Thirty is the minimum age to be a member of the council, not to vote.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many years' practice of the trade does the 1806 law require to sit on the Lyon council?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: To be a member of the council, one must show six years' practice of the trade, in addition to being at least thirty and able to read and write.
